(Define the weight of a graph to be the sum of the weights of the vertices and edges of that graph.)  prove this is NP-Complete

message.content: Let us begin. We prove NP-completeness of this problem. First, we show membership in NP for this problem. A certificate consists of a specific subgraph of the given graph G. We verify in polynomial time that the sum of vertex and edge weights equals k. Next, we will reduce from SUBSET SUM, a well-known NP-complete problem in the field of computational complexity theory. Given an instance of SUBSET SUM with integers a_1 through a_n and target value T, we construct a graph as follows. The constructed graph has exactly n vertices with no edges, where vertex i is assigned weight a_i for each i from 1 to n. We then set k equal to T, the target value from the SUBSET SUM instance, and ask whether this graph contains a subgraph of total weight k. Since the graph has no edges, any subgraph is simply a subset of vertices, and the weight of that subgraph is the sum of the weights of the chosen vertices. Therefore, the constructed graph contains a subgraph of weight k if and only if there exists a subset of the given integers that sums to exactly T, which is the SUBSET SUM question. This reduction is clearly polynomial in time, since we only need to create n isolated vertices and assign their respective weights, which takes at most O(n) time, making the entire construction polynomial in the input size. Since we have demonstrated both that the problem belongs to NP and that it is NP-hard through a valid polynomial-time reduction from the known NP-complete problem SUBSET SUM, we can now firmly conclude the Weighted Subgraph problem is NP-complete.
